title: Arion · lines 6–15
subtitle: At sea the crew plot to kill Arion for his money; given a choice of deaths, he asks to sing one last time

units.en: Out at sea, however, they plotted to throw Arion overboard and keep his money.

notes.label: σκευή
notes.body: Dress or equipment. Here it is the formal robes a citharode wore to perform at a festival or contest.

notes.label: The stern-deck
notes.body: The seats on the raised deck at the stern (the back) of the ship, where the helmsman sat to steer.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The setting comes first: the crew wait until they are on the open sea, where Arion has nowhere to escape to. This makes his danger feel inescapable.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The verb shows the crew scheming together in secret. It is the first sign of the treachery the reader was led to expect in lines 5–6.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Money is named twice in one line, first as what the sailors want and then as what Arion offers them. The repetition shows that wealth drives the whole conflict.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Arion understands and begins to plead in the space of three words. He grasps his danger at once, and the story keeps moving.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.body: Money is set against life: Arion will give up the one to keep the other. The balance shows what really matters to him.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The strong negative, sharpened by δή, shuts down his plea at once. The reader sees there is no hope of mercy.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.trans: either to kill himself … or to jump
notes.body: Two harsh options are linked by ἢ … ἢ, but it is a choice with no real choice in it: either way Arion dies.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The sailors want Arion to do the killing himself, so that their own hands stay clean. They are cowardly as well as cruel.

notes.label: Irony
notes.trans: so that he could be buried on land
notes.body: A grave on land is offered as if it were a kindness, though it comes with a demand that he die. The reader sees how callous the crew are.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: "As fast as possible" comes at the very end of the sentence, so the crew's impatience is the last thing we hear.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The participle opens the sentence, so before we even hear Arion's name we know he has been forced into a corner. ἀπορία means literally "no way through".

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Facing death, Arion asks to perform in his full costume: he still thinks like a professional musician. This makes him dignified and sympathetic.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The raised deck at the stern becomes his stage, and the reader can picture the scene of the last performance.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The verb "sing" appears twice, in different forms, side by side. The song is placed at the centre of the story.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Arion calmly promises to take his own life once he has sung. The reader pities a man who bargains for nothing more than a song.

questions: Why do you think the sailors give Arion a choice of deaths rather than simply killing him?
How does Herodotus make Arion's request seem dignified rather than desperate?
Which Greek words in these lines best convey the sailors' greed, and which their cruelty?
